nodes.description: Most of the CoQ10 biosynthesis enzymes act after side-chain attachment, on the benzoquinone ring, and may assemble into resolvable domains described as COQ complexes. COQ4, COQ5, COQ6, COQ7 and COQ9 act in this segment: COQ4 is the zinc-dependent C1 decarboxylase, COQ5 the pathway's C-methyltransferase, COQ6 its flavin-dependent ring monooxygenase, COQ7 the NADH-dependent demethoxyubiquinone hydroxylase, and COQ9 a lipid-binding protein that presents its bound lipid to COQ7. Biallelic defects in this segment therefore block CoQ10 maturation after the side chain has been attached.

evidence.snippet: The majority of these enzymes are responsible for modifications of the CoQ-head group (benzoquinone ring).

evidence.snippet: The head-modifying enzymes may assemble into resolvable domains, representing COQ complexes.

nodes.description: COQ8A and COQ8B are closely similar atypical kinases that support the CoQ10 biosynthetic machinery rather than being assigned a named chemical step of the pathway. COQ8B localises to the mitochondrial matrix of kidney podocytes and interacts with pathway members including COQ6 and COQ7, and COQ8A was established as a pathway participant before COQ8B was identified. Loss of COQ8B reduces cellular CoQ10 in patient-derived cells.

nodes.description: Biallelic pathogenic variants in any of the nuclear CoQ10 biosynthesis genes (PDSS1, PDSS2, COQ2, COQ4, COQ5, COQ6, COQ7, COQ8A, COQ8B, COQ9) reduce endogenous CoQ10 production, lowering tissue and cellular CoQ10 levels. This is the shared upstream lesion across all primary CoQ10 deficiency subtypes.

evidence.reference_title: Primary Coenzyme Q10 Deficiency: An Update.
evidence.snippet: In man, at least 10 genes are required for the biosynthesis of functional CoQ10, a mutation in any one of which can result in a deficit in CoQ10 status.

nodes.description: The first steps of CoQ10 biosynthesis build the polyisoprenoid tail and attach it to the 4-hydroxybenzoate ring. Only three of the disease genes act here: PDSS1 and PDSS2 each encode a subunit of the decaprenyl diphosphate synthase that supplies the side chain, and COQ2 is the polyprenyltransferase that joins it to the ring. Biallelic defects in this segment therefore block CoQ10 assembly at its earliest committed step, and the reported phenotypes of this segment include prominent visual involvement.

evidence.snippet: Only three enzymes (PDSS1, PDSS2 and COQ2) are required for assembly and attachment of the polyisoprenoid side chain.

The PDSS1 gene encodes prenyl diphosphate synthase subunit 1, an enzyme that supplies decaprenyl diphosphate, the precursor for the side chain of the isoprenoid quinone Coenzyme Q10 that functions as a mobile electron carrier in the respiratory chain, as well as other mitochondrial functions including antioxidant properties.

nodes.description: CoQ10 normally shuttles electrons from respiratory chain complexes I and II to complex III. Reduced CoQ10 impairs this electron transfer, decreasing oxidative phosphorylation and ATP synthesis, biochemically detectable as reduced combined complex I+III and II+III activities.

evidence.reference_title: Leigh syndrome with nephropathy and CoQ10 deficiency due to decaprenyl diphosphate synthase subunit 2 (PDSS2) mutations.
evidence.snippet: Coenzyme Q(10) (CoQ(10)) is a vital lipophilic molecule that transfers electrons from mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes I and II to complex III.

nodes.description: Beyond bioenergetics, CoQ10 is a lipid-soluble antioxidant and supports redox homeostasis, ferroptosis defense, and sulfide oxidation. Combined energy failure and loss of antioxidant/redox protection produce multisystem injury, with the nervous system, kidney, heart, and sensory organs particularly vulnerable. Neurologic injury involves neuronal death, neuroinflammation, and cerebral gliosis.
